lede: Every bottle of solution in a laboratory carries a label such as 0.2 mol/dm³: how much substance is dissolved in each cubic decimetre. The second half asks a different question. When you make a chemical, how much of what you start with ends up in the product you actually want?
can: Calculate a concentration in mol/dm³ from a mass of solute and a volume of solution.
Work out the moles or the mass of solute in a volume of known concentration.
Calculate an atom economy from a balanced equation and explain why a high one matters.

md: Make squash twice: one spoonful of powder in a small glass, then one spoonful in a full jug. Same powder, very different drinks, because the same amount is shared through more water. Chemists need to say exactly how strong a solution is, so they count the dissolved substance in moles and share it out per cubic decimetre.

caption: Four beakers like the one on the left would fill 1 dm³, so 1 dm³ of this solution holds four times the moles.

md: Read the picture from the left. One beaker holds 0.100 mol in 250 cm³. Four of them make a whole dm³, so a dm³ holds 4 × 0.100 = 0.400 mol. That number, **moles in each dm³**, is the concentration: 0.400 mol/dm³.

prompt: Two solutions each contain 0.1 mol of salt. One has a volume of 250 cm³ and the other 1000 cm³. Which is more concentrated?
explain: Concentration is the moles in each dm³. The same 0.1 mol is packed into a quarter of a dm³ in one and spread through a whole dm³ in the other, so each dm³ of the smaller solution holds four times as much. The 250 cm³ solution is more concentrated.

caption: A cubic decimetre is the volume of a cube 10 cm along each edge: one litre.

md:
**Concentration** is the number of moles of the dissolved substance, the **solute**, in each cubic decimetre of solution:
**concentration (mol/dm³) = moles ÷ volume (dm³)**
A cubic decimetre is a cube 10 cm along each edge, so 1 dm³ = 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000 cm³, which is one litre. Read mol/dm³ as *moles per cubic decimetre*.

explain: A cubic decimetre is a cube 10 cm along each edge, so it holds 10 × 10 × 10 small cubes of 1 cm³: 1000 cm³. Every conversion in this lesson uses that one number.

text: Why chemists count moles, not grams

md: Reactions happen particle by particle, and a mole of any substance is the same number of particles. So two solutions with the same concentration in mol/dm³ carry the same amount of substance to react in every dm³, even when their masses are very different. That is why CCEA asks for mol/dm³.

Two solutions, both 0.100 mol/dm³, compared dm³ for dm³:
**Sodium chloride:** 0.100 × 58.5 = 5.85 g in each dm³.
**Glucose:** 0.100 × 180 = 18.0 g in each dm³.
The masses differ; the moles, and so the amount available to react, are the same.

prompt: A glucose solution and a sodium chloride solution are both 0.100 mol/dm³. What is the same in each dm³ of the two solutions?
options: the number of moles of solute
both the mass and the moles of solute
answer: the number of moles of solute
explain: Both are 0.100 mol/dm³, so each dm³ holds 0.100 mol of solute. The masses differ because the formula masses differ: 5.85 g of sodium chloride against 18.0 g of glucose. So it is the moles that are the same.

md: Laboratory volumes are measured in cm³, but the formula needs dm³. So the first line of every concentration calculation is the conversion, written on its own: **divide cm³ by 1000**. Leave the volume in cm³ and a concentration comes out a thousand times too small, while a number of moles comes out a thousand times too big.

Three conversions, each dividing by 1000:
**A whole litre:** 1000 ÷ 1000 = 1 dm³.
**A beaker:** 250 ÷ 1000 = 0.250 dm³.
**A pipette:** 25.0 ÷ 1000 = 0.0250 dm³.
A dm³ is the bigger unit, so the number always gets smaller.

explain: A dm³ is a thousand times bigger than a cm³, so there are a thousand times fewer of them: divide by 1000. 75 ÷ 1000 = 0.075 dm³. If you reached 75 000, you multiplied instead of dividing.

text: From a mass to a concentration

caption: 5.85 g of sodium chloride, dissolved and made up to exactly 250 cm³.

md:
**The question.** 5.85 g of sodium chloride, NaCl, is dissolved and made up to 250 cm³ of solution. Calculate the concentration in mol/dm³.
**Line 1, the volume.** 250 ÷ 1000 = 0.250 dm³.
**Line 2, the moles.** The Mr of NaCl is 23 + 35.5 = 58.5, so moles = mass ÷ Mr = 5.85 ÷ 58.5.

prompt: Sodium chloride has Mr 58.5. How many moles are there in 5.85 g of it?
explain: Concentration counts moles, so the grams must become moles first: moles = mass ÷ Mr. 5.85 ÷ 58.5 = 0.100 mol. Keep it on its own line: in the exam it is a mark of its own even if the next line slips.

md:
**Line 3, the concentration.** moles ÷ volume = 0.100 ÷ 0.250 = **0.400 mol/dm³**.
Write all three lines even when the arithmetic feels easy. A slip in line 2 then costs one mark, not three, because the examiner follows your working forward.

prompt: 0.0400 mol of copper(II) sulfate is dissolved to make 0.200 dm³ of solution. What is its concentration in mol/dm³?
explain: Check the unit before you divide: the volume is already in dm³, so there is nothing to convert. Then concentration = moles ÷ volume = 0.0400 ÷ 0.200 = 0.200 mol/dm³.

text: Turning it round: moles and mass

alt: A triangle with moles at the top and concentration and volume in dm³ along the bottom: cover the quantity you want to see how to find it.
svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 260" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-labelledby="c4trit"><title id="c4trit">A triangle split into three: moles at the top, concentration at the bottom left and volume in dm³ at the bottom right. Cover the one you want: moles is concentration times volume; concentration is moles divided by volume; volume is moles divided by concentration.</title><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.4"><path d="M200 30 L350 230 L50 230 z"/><path d="M117.5 140 H282.5"/><path d="M200 140 V230"/></g><g font-family="inherit" font-size="15" fill="currentColor"><text x="200" y="118" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">moles</text><text x="137" y="204" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">conc.</text><text x="263" y="204" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">vol (dm³)</text><text x="200" y="254" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle">cover the one you want</text></g></svg>
caption: Cover the quantity you want: what is left says whether to multiply or divide.

md: When the concentration is known, rearrange: **moles = concentration × volume (dm³)**. If the question wants grams, finish with **mass = moles × Mr**.

For example, the mass of potassium nitrate, $\ce{KNO3}$, in 250 cm³ of a 0.400 mol/dm³ solution:
**Volume:** 250 ÷ 1000 = 0.250 dm³.
**Moles:** 0.400 × 0.250 = 0.100 mol.
**Mass:** Mr = 39 + 14 + 48 = 101, so 0.100 × 101 = **10.1 g**.

prompt: How many moles of solute are there in 50.0 cm³ of a 2.00 mol/dm³ solution?
explain: The concentration is the moles in each dm³, so multiply it by the number of dm³. Convert first: 50.0 cm³ = 0.0500 dm³. Then 2.00 × 0.0500 = 0.100 mol. Multiplying by 50.0 instead gives 100 mol, far more than a small beaker could hold.

title: PhET: Concentration

task: The concentration reading is in mol/L, and a litre is the same as a dm³. Choose copper sulfate, shake in solid until the reading is about 0.2 mol/L, then run in more water without adding any solid. Watch the reading, and write one sentence saying what happened to the concentration and why. (This simulation is for the concentration half of the lesson only.)

prompt: Water is added to a solution, but no more solute. What happens to its concentration?
explain: Concentration is moles ÷ volume. Adding water leaves the moles of solute the same but makes the volume bigger, so each dm³ holds fewer moles: the concentration goes down.

md: You never need to learn the three versions separately. Concentration is defined as the moles in each dm³, so it is found by sharing the moles out over the dm³.

**Share it out:** 0.600 mol in 1.50 dm³ gives 0.600 ÷ 1.50 = 0.400 mol in each dm³.
**Undo the sharing:** multiply both sides by the volume, so moles = concentration × volume.
**Undo it the other way:** divide by the concentration, so volume = moles ÷ concentration.

prompt: Starting from concentration = moles ÷ volume, which rearrangement gives the volume of a solution?
explain: Multiply both sides of concentration = moles ÷ volume by the volume to get moles = concentration × volume, then divide both sides by the concentration. That leaves volume = moles ÷ concentration, which the triangle shows by covering the volume.

text: Atom economy: where the atoms go

alt: Bars drawn to scale for heating calcium carbonate: 100 mass units of CaCO₃ become 56 of calcium oxide, the darker bar, and 44 of carbon dioxide, a lighter bar, so the atom economy is 56.0%.
svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 270" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-labelledby="c4flowlimestonemt"><title id="c4flowlimestonemt">Bars drawn to scale: the reactants CaCO₃ above, the products CaO + CO₂ below, the same total length because mass is conserved. The darker bar is CaO, calcium oxide, 56 of the 100, so the atom economy is 56.0%.</title><defs><marker id="c4flowlimestone" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto"><path d="M0 0 L10 5 L0 10 z" fill="currentColor"/></marker></defs><g fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.14" stroke="none"><rect x="20.0" y="34" width="360.0" height="52"/><rect x="221.6" y="148" width="158.4" height="52"/></g><g fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.42" stroke="none"><rect x="20.0" y="148" width="201.6" height="52"/></g><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.4"><rect x="20.0" y="34" width="360.0" height="52"/><rect x="20.0" y="148" width="201.6" height="52"/><rect x="221.6" y="148" width="158.4" height="52"/><path d="M200 92 V140" marker-end="url(#c4flowlimestone)"/></g><g font-family="inherit" font-size="14" fill="currentColor"><text x="20" y="26" font-weight="600">reactants</text><text x="210" y="128">products</text><text x="200.0" y="56" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">CaCO₃</text><text x="200.0" y="75" text-anchor="middle">100</text><text x="120.8" y="170" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">CaO</text><text x="120.8" y="189" text-anchor="middle">56</text><text x="300.8" y="170" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">CO₂</text><text x="300.8" y="189" text-anchor="middle">44</text><text x="20" y="222">darker: calcium oxide</text><text x="20" y="250" font-weight="600">atom economy = 56 ÷ 100 × 100 = 56.0%</text></g></svg>
caption: The products weigh exactly what the reactants weighed. Atom economy asks how much of it is the product you wanted.

md:
Most reactions make something besides the product you want. **Atom economy** measures how much of the products' mass is the product you want:
**atom economy = (mass of desired product ÷ total mass of products) × 100**
Heating limestone to make lime: $\ce{CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2}$. Of every 100 mass units, 56 become calcium oxide and 44 leave as carbon dioxide, so the atom economy is 56 ÷ 100 × 100 = 56%.

title: Why the equation settles it
md: Mass is conserved, so the products weigh as much as the reactants. The balanced equation therefore fixes the atom economy before any experiment: a by-product wastes its share of the atoms, however carefully the reaction is done.

prompt: Ethene and steam make ethanol and nothing else: C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH. What is the atom economy of this reaction?
options: it cannot be known without doing the experiment
explain: Atom economy is the desired product's share of the products' mass. Here the ethanol is the only product, so it is all of that mass: desired ÷ total = 1, and 1 × 100 = 100%. The equation fixes it; no experiment is needed.

md:
**The question.** In the blast furnace, $\ce{Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2}$. Calculate the atom economy for making iron, to one decimal place.
**Line 1, the desired product with its balancing number.** 2Fe: 2 × 56 = 112.
**Line 2, every product with its balancing number.** 3CO₂: 3 × 44 = 132, so the total is 112 + 132 = 244.

prompt: Finish the blast-furnace calculation: 112 ÷ 244 × 100, to one decimal place.
explain: Desired mass over total mass of products, times 100: 112 ÷ 244 × 100 = 45.9%. Dropping the 2 in front of Fe gives 23.0%; dropping the 3 in front of CO₂ gives 71.8%. Balancing numbers are part of the masses.

md:
**Line 3, the percentage.** 112 ÷ 244 × 100 = **45.9%**.
**A free check.** The reactants add up to 160 + 3 × 28 = 244 as well. If your two totals disagree, a balancing number has gone missing.

prompt: In the thermite reaction, 2Al + Fe₂O₃ → 2Fe + Al₂O₃. Iron is the product wanted. What goes on top of the atom economy fraction?
explain: The top line is the mass of the desired product, with its balancing number. The equation makes two iron atoms, so it is 2 × 56 = 112. Aluminium is a reactant, and a reactant never goes on top.

text: Why a high atom economy matters

md:
Copper(II) sulfate can be made from copper(II) oxide or from copper(II) carbonate. The carbonate route also makes carbon dioxide, so its atom economy is lower.
**From the oxide:** 160 ÷ 178 × 100 = 89.9%.
**From the carbonate:** 160 ÷ 222 × 100 = 72.1%.

A high atom economy matters for two separate reasons, and a full answer gives both.
**Sustainable development:** fewer raw materials are used up to make the same product, and less waste is made.
**Economic:** less money goes on raw materials that end up as waste, and on getting rid of it.

prompt: Which of these is a reason for wanting a high atom economy that an examiner would credit?
explain: Atom economy is about where the atoms go, so the reasons that earn marks are about atoms: less waste, fewer raw materials used up, and lower costs. Energy and speed are not part of it, so the answer is less waste.

title: Summer 2025 C2 Higher Q5
md: Asked why a laboratory preparation with a low atom economy was **not sustainable**, candidates struggled, and answers about **using less energy were not credited**. Argue from the atoms: raw materials used up, waste made, and what both cost.

title: GCSE Chemistry Revision "Atom Economy" (Triple)
why: A second explanation of the atom economy formula, worked on different reactions. 'Triple' in the title is another board's label: for CCEA this is Higher Tier Double Award content.

prompt: A company switches to a route with a higher atom economy. Which of these is an economic reason for the switch?
options: less is spent on raw materials that end up as waste
fewer resources are used up for future generations
answer: less is spent on raw materials that end up as waste
explain: Economic means money, and sustainable development means resources and waste for the future. Only the first answer is about money: less spent on raw materials that end up as waste. A full answer to 'why does it matter' gives one of each kind.

text: See it done: a Higher chain

md:
Higher papers join the two halves in one question. Here is the chain at writing speed.
**Moles needed:** 200 cm³ of 0.500 mol/dm³, so 0.500 × 0.200 = 0.100 mol.
**Mr:** MgCl₂ = 24 + (2 × 35.5) = 95.
**Mass:** 0.100 × 95 = 9.50 g.

Then the atom economy for making the salt, $\ce{Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + H2}$:
**Desired:** MgCl₂ = 95.
**Total:** 95 + 2 = 97.
**Show that it is about 97.9%:** 95 ÷ 97 × 100 = 97.94%.

prompt: To find the mass of solute needed for a solution of known volume and concentration, what do you work out first?
options: the moles: concentration × volume in dm³
the mass: concentration × volume in cm³
the Mr divided by the volume
answer: the moles: concentration × volume in dm³
explain: The concentration tells you the moles in each dm³, so the first line is the moles: concentration × volume in dm³. Only then does the Mr turn moles into grams. Using the volume in cm³ makes the answer a thousand times too big.

md: **The relative atomic masses are printed in the question.** Higher papers often list them beside the calculation. Use them: they are the Data Leaflet's values, and your Mr must be built from them.

**'Show that the atom economy is …'.** The answer is given, so the marks are for the lines: the desired mass, the total mass of products, then the division, ending on more figures than the value printed.

**'What else would you need?'** A paper gave a concentration and a volume, then asked what was missing to find the mass. Work it through:
**Moles:** 0.150 × 0.300 = 0.0450 mol.
**Mass:** 0.0450 × Mr, so the missing piece is the relative formula mass.

prompt: A question gives the concentration and the volume of a solution and asks what other information you need to find the mass of solute in it. What is the answer?
options: the relative formula mass (Mr) of the solute
the volume in cm³ as well as in dm³
answer: the relative formula mass (Mr) of the solute
explain: Concentration × volume gives the moles, and mass = moles × Mr. So the one thing still needed is the relative formula mass of the solute; temperature plays no part, and the volume is already given.

md: **'Dissolved in 500 cm³ of water'.** Treat the volume given as the volume of the solution; convert it to dm³ as usual.

**'Explain why this method is not sustainable'.** Start from the number: an atom economy of 40% means 100 − 40 = 60% of the products' mass is waste. So more raw materials are used up, and more waste made, for each gram of product. Energy was not credited in 2025.

prompt: A laboratory preparation has an atom economy of only 19%. Which answer earns the mark for why it is not sustainable?
options: most of the mass of the reactants ends up as waste, so raw materials are used up
it needs a lot of energy to heat the reactants
the reaction is too slow to be useful
answer: most of the mass of the reactants ends up as waste, so raw materials are used up
explain: A 19% atom economy means 81% of the products' mass is not the product wanted: it is waste, and the raw materials that made it are used up. That is what sustainability is about here. Energy and speed were not credited.

text: Going further: yield is not atom economy

md: Both are percentages, and they answer different questions. **Atom economy** comes from the balanced equation: how much of the products' mass is the product you want. **Percentage yield** comes from an experiment: how much product you actually collected, compared with the most you could have made.

Heating 50.0 g of calcium carbonate can make at most 28.0 g of calcium oxide.
**Yield:** 21.0 g collected, so 21.0 ÷ 28.0 × 100 = 75.0%.
**Atom economy:** 56 ÷ 100 × 100 = 56.0%, however much is collected.

title: Where the specification stops
md: Every concentration on your paper is in mol/dm³. Concentrations in g/dm³ and calculations from titrations are not on this specification.

prompt: Heating calcium carbonate gives a 100% yield of calcium oxide. What is the atom economy for making calcium oxide?
explain: The yield comes from the experiment and the atom economy from the equation. A 100% yield means every possible gram of calcium oxide was collected, but the equation still sends 44 of every 100 mass units away as carbon dioxide. So the atom economy stays 56%.

md:
Convert cm³ to dm³ first, then find a concentration from a mass and a volume.
Find the moles or the mass of solute in a solution of known concentration.
Calculate an atom economy, balancing numbers included, and show that a given value is right.
Give a sustainable-development and an economic reason for a high atom economy, never energy.
Tell atom economy, from the equation, from percentage yield, from the experiment.

This is Higher Tier only, and the two halves often share one question. A mass or concentration is **[2]** to **[3]**: the volume in dm³ and the moles first, the Mr, then the answer. An atom economy is **[3]**: the desired mass, the total mass of products, the percentage. Write every line, because a slip is carried forward. For *not sustainable*, argue from wasted atoms and cost, never energy.
